clue.text: Working on charter airline carrying first-class towards Heathrow Terminal 5, e.g.

indicators.note: an airline carrying passengers holds them inside, so the airline's letters go round the next pieces

parts.note: TUI is a holiday company that runs charter flights
best means first-class, top quality
at, as in 'aim at', means towards
on means working, as a machine that is on

explanation.surface: A holiday charter flight brings a first-class passenger to Heathrow's newest terminal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Working on' puts ON at the end. TUI is a British-based package-holiday firm with its own charter airline.
explanation.definitionFit: Heathrow Terminal 5 has its own stop on London's Underground, the Piccadilly line, so it is an example.

clue.text: Prisoner under sentence causes delay

indicators.note: in a down clue, a piece under another comes after it

parts.note: time is a prison sentence, as in 'doing time'
a lag is a convict, especially an old lag

explanation.surface: A convict serving a sentence holds things up.
explanation.definitionFit: A time lag is an interval between one event and another, a holdup in time.

clue.text: Lad penning books to get prize

indicators.note: penning means shutting in, so the lad's letters enclose the books

parts.note: a lad is a boy
OT is the Old Testament, a set of books

explanation.surface: A boy writes books to win a prize.
explanation.walkthrough: Penning looks like writing but means enclosing.
explanation.definitionFit: Booty is plunder taken in war or theft, a prize seized by the victor.

clue.text: Red wine lake lowered somewhat — supporting prices, finally

indicators.note: in a down clue the supporting piece sits beneath, so the wine piece goes below the end of prices
finally points to the last letter of prices
the lake letter is moved a little further down the word

parts.note: claret is red wine from Bordeaux
L is the map abbreviation for lake

explanation.surface: A glut of red wine has been discounted somewhat, which props up prices.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wine lake' suggests the EU's old wine surplus, but lake just supplies the letter that sinks within the wine word.
explanation.definitionFit: Scarlet is a vivid shade of the colour red.

clue.text: Protected from breaking into unpoliced metal packing

indicators.note: the Met, London's Metropolitan Police, is taken away from the word metal

parts.note: packing is slang for carrying a gun, armed

explanation.surface: Something about metal smuggled through without police checks.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition runs to 'breaking into': a building fitted with a burglar alarm is protected against a break-in.
explanation.definitionFit: A building that is alarmed has a security system fitted to deter burglars.

clue.text: Suggest variable annuities

indicators.note: variable means changeable, so the letters of annuities change their order

explanation.surface: Financial advice recommending annuities whose payouts vary.
explanation.definitionFit: To insinuate is to hint at something indirectly, an implying of it.

clue.text: Disgusting number one — very much my sort of thing

parts.note: I is the Roman numeral for one

parts.words: very much my sort of thing
parts.note: 'so me' is a phrase meaning that thing really suits me

explanation.surface: Someone praises a revolting thing as their number one, totally their style.
explanation.definitionFit: Noisome means offensive or foul-smelling, a revolting quality, not loud.

clue.text: Romp cut short by case of listeria — it's a game of chance

indicators.note: a word cut short loses its final letter, here the tail of the romp word

parts.note: an old sense of romp is a lively, boisterous girl, a tomboy

indicators.note: a word's case is its outer shell, so only the first and last letters of listeria are taken

explanation.surface: A frolic interrupted by a bout of listeria, oddly called a game of chance.
explanation.walkthrough: Romp in the sense of a tomboyish girl is an old dictionary meaning few solvers know.
explanation.definitionFit: A tombola is a raffle drawing tickets from a revolving drum, purely a matter of luck.

clue.text: Somehow still barely seventeen, for example

indicators.note: somehow means by some unexplained means, so these letters are rearranged in an unstated way

explanation.surface: Someone who is still only just seventeen years old.
explanation.walkthrough: Seventeen looks like an age, but it is a word with three syllables: sev-en-teen.
explanation.definitionFit: A trisyllable is a word with three syllables, and the number word splits into three spoken parts.

clue.text: Alcoholic's lies backfire about bottles — heads to rock bottom?

indicators.note: about can mean turned round, so the concealed run of letters is read backwards
the clue phrase bottles, or holds within it, the letters needed

explanation.surface: A drinker's falsehoods come back to bite them once the drink is involved.
explanation.walkthrough: Inside 'Alcoholic's lies backfire' sits SLIESBA; 'about' turns it round. The question mark flags that the definition is playful.
explanation.definitionFit: A climber who descends a cliff by rope is literally heading down towards the foot of the rock.

clue.text: It shows what one's up to when Saint Peter is welcoming journalist over me

definitions.text: It shows what one's up to

indicators.note: welcoming means letting in, so Peter's letters surround what follows

parts.note: ED is short for editor, a journalist
O is the cricket abbreviation for over

explanation.surface: At the pearly gates, Saint Peter greets a reporter ahead of the speaker.
explanation.walkthrough: S plus PETER holding ED, O and ME gives S-PE-EDOME-TER. 'What one's up to' is the speed you have reached.
explanation.definitionFit: A speedometer is the dial that shows a vehicle's current speed, how fast one is going.

clue.text: Ornamental work where daughter goes to become well-mannered woman?

indicators.note: this says what the daughter's letter turns the song word into: a lady, a polite woman

parts.note: D, the abbreviation for daughter, goes into a word for a song or ballad; the answer names where it went, read as two words

explanation.surface: A finishing-school question: where should a daughter be sent to turn out a lady?
explanation.walkthrough: Read the answer as two words, IN LAY: put D (daughter) in LAY and you get LADY.
explanation.definitionFit: Inlay is decoration set into a surface, such as wood or ivory sunk into furniture.

clue.text: European newspaper, ultimately fated to become Spain's Sun — one found by schoolmate?

indicators.note: one letter is told to become something else, so it is swapped out for new letters

parts.note: Le Monde is the leading French daily paper

indicators.note: ultimately points to the last letter of fated

parts.note: sol is Spanish for sun

explanation.surface: A European paper's fate is to turn into a Spanish tabloid, apparently.
explanation.walkthrough: In LE MONDE the D (the end of fated) becomes SOL. A school is a shoal of fish, so a fish's schoolmate is another fish.
explanation.definitionFit: The lemon sole is a flatfish, and fish swim in schools, so it is found beside its schoolmates.

clue.text: Kinky orgy with UHT milk product

indicators.note: kinky means twisted, so these letters are bent into a new order

parts.note: taken as written; UHT is ultra-heat-treated milk

explanation.surface: A racy gathering featuring long-life milk, presented as if it were a dairy item.
explanation.definitionFit: Yoghurt is made by fermenting milk with bacteria, a dairy food.

clue.text: Encouraging noises from courier — last drop from delivery is in time

definitions.note: the answer is an exclamation said to a child who stumbles, so it stands for such cheering sounds

parts.note: UPS is a parcel delivery firm

indicators.note: the last letter is dropped from the word delivery and taken
in means the word is goes inside the time word

parts.note: a day is a period of time

explanation.surface: A courier makes reassuring noises as the last parcel arrives on time.
explanation.walkthrough: UPS is the American parcel firm United Parcel Service; 'delivery' belongs to its surface but only lends its final letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Upsy-daisy is the comforting phrase said while lifting a small child who has fallen, an encouragement.

clue.text: Late goal creates stalemate

parts.note: the late someone is someone dead
an end is an aim or goal

explanation.surface: A last-minute goal produces a deadlock in a match.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Late goal' reads as football, but late is the dead sense.
explanation.definitionFit: A dead end is a situation with no way forward, a deadlock where progress stops.

clue.text: Payment from Pinter's script, primarily defined by large breaks in speech

parts.note: L is the clothing-size abbreviation for large

indicators.note: something defined by its bounds is enclosed by them, so the initials sit inside

parts.note: um and um are hesitations, pauses in speaking

indicators.note: primarily means first, so each word's first letter is taken

explanation.surface: Harold Pinter's plays are famous for their long pauses, here supposedly the source of a fee.
explanation.walkthrough: Harold Pinter was a British playwright noted for his pauses, which makes 'breaks in speech' apt for his script.
explanation.definitionFit: A lump sum is a single payment of the whole amount at once rather than in instalments.

clue.text: Joined political journalist with something incendiary

parts.note: Andrew Marr is a British political journalist and broadcaster
an IED, an improvised explosive device, is something that blows up

explanation.surface: A political reporter teams up with something inflammatory.
explanation.definitionFit: Married means united as a couple, or more generally linked together.

clue.text: Perhaps Mourinho's hair embracing silver colour at last

indicators.note: embracing means holding within, so the hair word wraps round the silver symbol

parts.note: a mane is a long head of hair
Ag is the chemical symbol for silver

indicators.note: at last points to the final letter of colour

explanation.surface: José Mourinho's hair, going grey, is described in detail.
explanation.walkthrough: José Mourinho is a famous Portuguese football coach, known for his greying hair.
explanation.definitionFit: Mourinho is a football manager, so he is an example of the person in charge of a team.

clue.text: Spy from the East meets Greek character and Bond's boss — shh!

indicators.note: in an across clue, coming from the east means reading from the right, backwards

parts.note: to peek is to spy or peep
mu is a letter of the Greek alphabet
M is James Bond's chief in the 007 stories

explanation.surface: A Cold War spy scene: an eastern agent, a Greek and M, all urging silence.
explanation.definitionFit: To keep mum is an idiom meaning stay silent, the same instruction as hushing someone.

clue.text: Bone needing potassium — nurse on the counter putting measurement up

parts.note: K is the chemical symbol for potassium

indicators.note: counter means going against the usual direction, so the nurse's letters are reversed

parts.note: EN is an enrolled nurse

indicators.note: in a down clue putting a word up reads it from the bottom, reversed

parts.note: a pace is a unit for measuring distance by stride

explanation.surface: A medical scene: a bone injury needs potassium and a nurse at the counter takes measurements.
explanation.walkthrough: 'On the counter' suggests a shop counter, but it means backwards.
explanation.definitionFit: The kneecap, or patella, is the small flat bone at the front of the knee joint.

clue.text: Regularly email heads about English transcript

indicators.note: regularly means taking every other letter, here the second and fourth of email
about means going round, so the heads word surrounds the English letter

parts.note: nuts is slang for heads

explanation.surface: Instructions on regularly emailing department heads about an English transcript.
explanation.definitionFit: Minutes are the written record of what was said at a meeting, a formal account.

clue.text: Northern poet's entertaining spots with clubs moved to later social event

indicators.note: a host entertaining a guest holds them within, so the poet's letters go round the northern letter

parts.note: acne is a rash of spots

explanation.walkthrough: 'Northern poet' suggests a single figure, but the two words give separate pieces, one tucked inside the other.
explanation.definitionFit: A barn dance is a country gathering with folk dancing, originally held in a farm building.

clue.text: Belief it could go either way

parts.note: this phrase says the answer reads the same in both directions, its own reverse

explanation.surface: A principle that someone might reasonably hold or abandon.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Could go either way' sounds like doubt, but it means the word reads the same forwards and backwards.
explanation.definitionFit: A tenet is a principle or doctrine that a person or group holds to be true.

clue.text: Short — sitting in booster seat

indicators.note: the answer sits inside the phrase booster seat, across the word gap

explanation.surface: A small child, too short to see over, is sat in a booster seat.
explanation.definitionFit: Terse means brief and to the point, using few words.

clue.text: Leaving dramatic chapter out

indicators.note: out means the chapter letter is removed

parts.note: exciting means dramatic, thrilling

explanation.surface: A tense scene cut from a book as a character departs.
explanation.definitionFit: Exiting means going out of a place, the same as departing.

clue.text: Copper with hobby, say, ignoring pressure to make superintendent

parts.note: Cu is the chemical symbol for copper

indicators.note: ignoring means leaving the pressure letter out

parts.note: the hobby is a small falcon, an example of a bird of prey
P is the physics symbol for pressure

explanation.surface: A policeman with a pastime who skips the pressure to win promotion to superintendent.
explanation.walkthrough: Copper and superintendent suggest police, but copper is Cu and hobby is a falcon, not a pastime.
explanation.definitionFit: A curator is the keeper in charge of a museum or gallery collection, one who oversees it.

clue.text: Pickpockets casing area try jostling tourists

explanation.definitionFit: Day-trippers are visitors who go somewhere for one day only, a kind of tourist.
